topic: Stapler: why do staple legs bend inward? (the head lowers onto the paper, a thin driver blade pushes the front staple through the sheets, two curved clinching grooves in the metal anvil steer the leg tips sideways so the legs fold under the paper toward each other)
principle: The anvil under the paper is a forming die: its two curved clinching grooves catch the staple's leg tips as the blade drives the staple through the sheets and curl each leg toward the other, flat under the paper, so the staple cannot slip back out.

firstComment:
Answer: they bend outward instead 🔧

When you press a stapler, the magazine stops on the paper and a thin steel blade keeps going: it pushes the front staple out and straight through the sheets. Under the paper sits the anvil, a small metal plate with two curved grooves. Each leg tip runs into a groove, the curve steers it sideways, and the leg folds under the paper toward the other leg. Folded under, the staple can't slip back out.

On most modern staplers the anvil can be rotated or slid to a second setting. Then the legs bend outward: that's "pinning", a temporary staple that holds but is easy to remove.

(Simplified 3D model, enlarged and cut open. Real staplers and staples vary.)

Sources:
Wikipedia, Stapler (permanent fastening drives the staple into an anvil, a small metal plate that bends the ends, usually inward; on most modern staplers the anvil rotates or slides to change between bending the ends inward for permanent stapling or outward for pinning; pinning is easily removed): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stapler
US patent 4,315,589, Stapler apparatus (the magazine stops on the anvil and the blade-like driver drives the outermost staple; the anvil has clinching grooves for bending the legs of a staple inwardly; the leg is curled to press against the bottom of the paper): https://patents.google.com/patent/US4315589

voiceover: Why do staple legs bend inward?
Straight legs would just slip back out of the paper.
Press down, and a thin blade drives the staple through.
Under the paper, the metal anvil has two curved grooves. They catch the tips and bend them in.
Folded under, the staple can't slip out.
